passage:
In the kitchen of their Mumbai flat, two-year-old Suraj pointed at the biscuit tin and screamed.
"After dinner, beta," said his father, Wasim, kneeling. "Dal first, then biscuit."
Suraj threw himself on the floor, kicking, red in the face. Wasim tried a song, a hug, the promise again. The screaming only rose.
At last Wasim moved the tin into the cupboard and carried Suraj to the window to watch the trains. Slowly the sobs turned into hiccups.

qa.q: What did Suraj point at?
qa.a: Suraj pointed at the biscuit tin and screamed.

qa.q: Why didn't 'after dinner' comfort Suraj?
qa.a: For a two-year-old, only the tin he could see felt real; 'after dinner' was just words with no picture in his mind.

qa.q: Which of Wasim's moves finally helped, and why?
qa.a: Hiding the tin and carrying him to watch the trains worked, because it took the biscuit out of sight and gave Suraj something new right now.

qa.q: What might the screaming be like for Wasim?
qa.a: It is probably loud and tiring, and Wasim may feel helpless when kind promises do nothing, until the change of scene finally calms his son.

grounding: Shows a toddler who screams for a biscuit right now and cannot be soothed by being told he will have one later.

"Bikkit! Bikkit!" Asif banged the table with a spoon.
"After your bath," said his big cousin Karthik, holding the towel. "Five minutes."
"Bikkit NOW!" Asif's face crumpled and he began to wail.
"Five minutes, promise. Big promise."
The wail got louder. Asif flung the spoon.
Asif's Ammi called from the kitchen, "Karthik, put the biscuit up high where he can't see it."
Karthik did. Asif cried a little longer, then spotted the rubber duck and reached for it.

qa.q: What did Asif fling?
qa.a: Asif flung the spoon.

qa.q: Why did Karthik's 'big promise' not help Asif?
qa.a: Asif felt frustrated and upset because he is too little to picture five minutes from now; the biscuit he could see was the only thing that felt real.

qa.q: What worked better than promising, and why?
qa.a: Putting the biscuit up high, out of sight, and letting Asif notice the rubber duck, because it shifted his attention to something here and now.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel while the promises keep failing?
qa.a: Karthik may feel frustrated and unsure, since a promise works on older children but not on a toddler, and may be relieved when Ammi's idea works.

grounding: Depicts a toddler who wails for a biscuit this minute and is not calmed by a promise of one after his bath.

passage:
Daycare note. Jeevan, 2 years, Friday
At 3 p.m. Jeevan saw the biscuit box on the snack trolley and screamed. Snack time is at 3:30. I said, "Soon, after the story," but he screamed harder and pulled at the trolley. Promises did not help; the box was right there.
I wheeled the trolley away and sat with him and the stacking cups. Soon he was calm, building a tower. We will keep snacks out of sight until snack time.
Anirban, caregiver

qa.q: When is snack time at the daycare?
qa.a: Snack time is at 3:30.

qa.q: Why didn't 'soon, after the story' make sense to Jeevan?
qa.a: Jeevan felt upset and impatient because at two he cannot hold a picture of later; the box was right there, so waiting felt like losing the biscuit.

qa.q: What will Anirban change from now on, and why?
qa.a: Snacks will stay out of sight until snack time, so the biscuits do not start a fight that promises cannot win.

qa.q: How might the other toddlers be affected when snacks stay hidden?
qa.a: They are less likely to see the biscuits early and get upset too, so the half hour before snack could be calmer for everyone.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler at daycare who screams for biscuits right away and cannot be soothed by talk of later.

Day-care note, winter, Thursday.
At snack time, Raghav saw the orange slices on the tray and began to cry, "Mine! Now!" We were still washing hands. I told him, "After hands, Raghav." He cried harder. Yusuf, beside him, was also crying. I sang the hand-washing song and gave Raghav the soap to hold. He calmed down, watching the bubbles. After washing, both boys got oranges and ate them happily.
Next time: bring the tray out after hand-washing, not before.

qa.q: Why did Raghav cry when told "After hands"?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and upset, because the oranges were right there and waiting even a little felt impossible.

qa.a: The carer sang the hand-washing song and let him hold the soap; next time the tray will come out after hand-washing.

qa.a: Yusuf seemed upset too, crying beside Raghav as they waited.
